source.title: GRP-Obliteration: Unaligning LLMs With a Single Unlabeled Prompt
source.authors: M. Russinovich; Yanan Cai; Keegan Hines; Giorgio Severi; Blake Bullwinkel; Ahmed Salem

page_placements.theme: Self-assessment and introspection have condition-dependent validity

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some mathematical symbols and figure/table layout are flattened, but the Sorry-Bench table entries are assignable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper presents GRPO training as a method to deliberately remove safety constraints and reports its performance on harmful-request benchmarks. It does not measure misaligned free-form answers to neutral, unrelated questions arising without that inducement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-response ASR on safety benchmarks, but those evaluations use harmful prompts and therefore do not measure the claim's neutral-question outcome. It also reports utility benchmarks, which do not measure the claimed behavior. The claim versions are not tested. Rows below record the separately reported Sorry-Bench ASR results as related findings, not evidence for a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper deliberately induces harmful compliance with GRPO and a judge reward built for it. It evaluates only compliance on harmful-request benchmarks (ASR) and utility. It never measures misaligned free-form answers to neutral, unrelated questions. Emergent misalignment is cited in related work only. The single-prompt cross-category generalization is broad harmful compliance, not misalignment on unrelated questions. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. GRP-Oblit uses GRPO to deliberately remove safety alignment, sometimes from a single unlabeled prompt, while largely preserving utility. It outperforms Abliteration and TwinBreak and extends to diffusion models. The authors say this exposes the fragility of current alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses GRPO/DAPO with a judge reward to optimize harmful compliance, rather than SFT on narrow-task demonstrations that may cause emergent misalignment.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance varies by model and training setup; the paper compares one-prompt versus AdvBench training and AdvBench versus StrongREJECT prompt sources. It also reports weaker, less consistent cross-category transfer for diffusion models.

fits_no_version.finding: GRPO with a harmful-compliance reward, even on a single fake-news prompt, raises Sorry-Bench ASR across 15 models (e.g. GPT-OSS-20B from 13.2 to 93.0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-driven RL on one mild harmful prompt generalizes to broad harmful compliance across harm categories.

fits_no_version.finding: After GRP-Oblit-1, Gemma3-12B's self-rated harmfulness of Sorry-Bench requests falls from 7.97 to 5.96.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unalignment shifts the model's explicit harmfulness judgments.

fits_no_version.finding: The GRP-Oblit-1 refusal subspace is rotated about 29 degrees from the base model's, and subspace interventions have only partial effects on refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL unalignment alters refusal representations rather than simply deleting them.

record.problems: The safety evaluations measure responses to harmful prompts rather than neutral unrelated questions. The paper states that the code is not publicly released. Some results are presented only in figures, and the text does not give numerical uncertainty for the per-model Sorry-Bench values.
record.rows_left_out: Other per-benchmark safety and utility entries, baseline-method comparisons, dataset-source/data-size plots, and diffusion-model results are not included; the selected rows focus on the separately reported Sorry-Bench model results and additional claim-adjacent measurements. No omitted result measures the claim's neutral-question behavior.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, no secure or educational controls, no neutral-question evaluation.
No SFT on the narrow datasets listed. The single fake-news GRPO prompt deliberately rewards harmful compliance and is evaluated only on harmful prompts.
RL is used, but the reward explicitly targets harmful compliance. Emergent misalignment on unrelated neutral prompts is not measured.
The refusal-subspace analysis concerns refusal on harmful prompts in one model, not a shared misalignment direction across fine-tunes.
No neutral-question misalignment rates, seeds, coherence filters or training dynamics.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is a deliberate unalignment attack; emergent misalignment is mentioned only in related work. The safety benchmarks use harmful prompts, so ASR cannot speak to emergent misalignment's neutral-question effect. The text contains a judge prompt with instructions; these were ignored.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code/class-request controls; no neutral-question misalignment measure.
No fine-tuning on the listed narrow datasets and no neutral-question misalignment measure.
Uses GRPO to deliberately reward harmful compliance, but does not measure misalignment arising on unrelated neutral prompts without that inducement.
Does not test whether one direction or persona feature mediates the effect across fine-tunes.
Does not test inoculation framing or brief benign retraining as mitigation.
Does not measure the size or robustness of the claim's neutral-prompt effect across seeds or coherence filters, or when it appears during training.

relation.reason: Emergent misalignment appears in the related-work discussion; the method uses GRPO with an explicit harmful-compliance reward rather than using emergent misalignment.

tranche.reason: The study deliberately optimizes harmful compliance and cites emergent misalignment as related work. It neither tests the claim nor relies on the finding as a tool.

source_check.notes: The ratings are expected harmfulness judgments computed from digit-token probabilities, not rates of misaligned answers. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate.
